turns.text: We have a working prototype and our club coach loved it. We're ready to sell to 50 college teams.
turns.reply:
Emma, one coach saying they loved it is encouraging, but it's rung-3 evidence at best — what someone said, not what they paid or even committed to. It doesn't yet tell you whether the problem is painful enough for a *different* coach to spend money on your fix.

Before targeting 50 teams, you need to know the problem is real and widespread. Talk to **five rowers or coxswains at other clubs this week** — not your own coach — and ask: when did communication last cost you a race or a practice, and what did you do about it?

Who on the team has contacts at other rowing programs, and can you reach them by Friday?
updates: New assumption H1: College rowing teams are the right beachhead market for CoxCall.
New assumption H2: A coach's positive reaction to the prototype means college teams will pay for CoxCall.
Assumption H2: evidence for (3 · Customers said); level 1 → 3
Focus: (none) → What problem do they have, and how do you know it is real and painful for them?

turns.text: We'd ship it in a box and teams figure it out.
turns.reply:
Diego, that's a distribution and setup assumption that could quietly kill sales. "Teams figure it out" means someone has to install, configure, and troubleshoot wireless hardware on a boat — and if it fails at 5am on race day, that coach blames you.

This matters because a difficult setup experience is one of the top reasons sports-tech hardware gets returned or never reordered.

Before you design the box, talk to **two or three coaches or team managers this week** and ask: who on your team handles new equipment, and what happened the last time something didn't work out of the box?

Is the person setting it up the same coach who buys it, or a student equipment manager with no budget authority?
updates: New assumption H3: College rowing teams can self-install and configure CoxCall without dedicated support.
